summary: Give the MAGI calculator the adjusted gross income, the foreign-earned income, the foreign housing cost and the non-taxable social benefits and it returns modified adjusted gross income (MAGI). It is built for a budget, a loan conversation, a payslip check or a what-if before you talk to a lender. Nothing is submitted anywhere: the arithmetic runs in the page you are looking at.

sections.title: How does the MAGI calculator work?
sections.html:
The MAGI calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports modified adjusted gross income (MAGI) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the adjusted gross income (AGI), the foreign-earned income, the foreign housing cost and the non-taxable social benefits.

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

sections.title: The formula behind the MAGI calculator
sections.html:
One relationship drives the whole page:

Modified adjusted gross income (MAGI)=(adjusted gross income (AGI) + employer-paid adoption benefits + foreign-earned income − foreign housing cost + IRA contributions + non-taxable social benefits + others + passive income or losses + savings bond interest + (1 ÷ 2) × self-employment taxes + student loan interest + qualified tuition expenses and fees)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Suppose Adjusted gross income (AGI) = 10, Foreign-earned income = 10, Foreign housing cost = 10 and Non-taxable social benefits = 10. Working through the relationship above gives Modified adjusted gross income (MAGI) = 95.

Read it as a template. Every number above can be replaced with one of yours; only the relationship between them is fixed.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Modified adjusted gross income (MAGI) = 95 should be roughly the size you expected from Adjusted gross income (AGI) = 10 and Foreign-earned income = 10.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• Shown in US Dollar, and convertible to any of the 113 units on that chip.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The MAGI calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Comparing two offers that quote their costs in different ways
  • Sizing up a purchase before you commit to it
  • Building a monthly budget and testing how one number shifts the rest
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the adjusted gross income, the foreign-earned income and the foreign housing cost — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.

faq.q: What does the MAGI calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns modified adjusted gross income (MAGI), derived from the adjusted gross income, the foreign-earned income and the foreign housing cost. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the MAGI calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the adjusted gross income, the foreign-earned income, the foreign housing cost and the non-taxable social benefits, which is 12 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter adjusted gross income (AGI) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Adjusted gross income (AGI) opens in US Dollar and the chip beside it offers 113 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Modified adjusted gross income (MAGI) = 95. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the MAGI calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — press Calculate and every result updates together.
